WHAT CHANGED, AND NOTHING ELSE. One file: `/Users/timothystockstill/code/macos/4thWAIV/agent-guard/.claude/worktrees/kit-walkthrough-targets/ts/metalang/render.test.ts`, and inside it only the `HARNESS` string in `describe('what a drawn page says about being narrated')`. No production code, no other test, no rule, nothing under `.agents/`. The confirmed finding was the only item in the round and it is the only thing fixed.

THE FIX, IN ORDER. The harness now (1) waits until the document reads `complete` before importing the bundle, which the DOM library reaches only after it has delivered its own `DOMContentLoaded`, so that event is spent before the bundle exists; (2) when the case is `announced`, registers the announcement as its own `DOMContentLoaded` listener BEFORE `await import(entry)`, so listener order puts the announcement on the window ahead of the bundle's single `{ once: true }` reading, whichever event carries it; (3) imports the bundle, waits for the draw, then dispatches the `DOMContentLoaded` and `load` it always dispatched. That is the shape the direction named, plus the parse wait that makes it deterministic: without the wait, the library's event could still land during the import and write the announcement BEFORE the bundle mounted, which would quietly retire the mount mutation. With it, no `DOMContentLoaded` exists between the parse and the dispatch, so the announcement is still written after mount — mutation 1 fails the announced case, as it must.

WHAT A REVIEWER SHOULD CHECK AND WILL FIND HOLDS. The browser order the earlier round pinned is preserved: mount with nothing said about narration, then the helper announces, then the reading. What changed is only how the announcement is delivered — a listener instead of a global written between two awaits. The page's bundle is unchanged and still registers one `{ once: true }` listener on `document`; the only difference it can see is that the announcement is already on the window when its listener runs.

ONE SMALL CLEANUP INSIDE THE SAME STRING. The parse wait would have been a second copy of the harness's existing wait loop (`for (let i = 0; i < n && !cond; i += 1) await tick()` plus a loud throw), so both now go through one `waitFor(done, saying, ticks)` in the harness. Each caller keeps its own patience unchanged — 200 ticks for the draw, as before, 2000 for the parse — and both still fail loudly with the message they always had. Behaviour identical, duplication not introduced.
